prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: Link Inventory Audit — Q1 2025 (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 7 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Page title" · longest unbreakable word 100px · one-line width 319px
  col 2: header "URL" · longest unbreakable word 324px · one-line width 841px
  col 3: header "Last checked" · longest unbreakable word 61px · one-line width 96px
  col 4: header "Status code" · longest unbreakable word 47px · one-line width 86px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 720px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 719px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 720px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Audit a set of pages by associating each page and URL with its latest check date and HTTP status.","reading":"Readers scan page titles to find an entry, then follow the row across to its URL, check date, and status; they may also scan dates and status codes down their columns for stale or problematic links.","groups":["Page title and URL identify the same resource; the title supports recognition and the URL provides the exact destination.","Last checked and Status code describe the audit result; compact adjacent columns make dates and outcomes easy to compare."],"keep_intact":["URL characters and their order must remain exact, even if a URL wraps across lines.","Dates and status codes should remain intact where possible for quick comparison.","Individual words in page titles should remain intact."],"may_wrap":["Page titles can wrap at spaces without losing meaning.","URLs may wrap at valid break opportunities; their long unbreakable segments need sufficient width to avoid overflow or forced breaking.","Header labels can wrap if necessary, and shorter cells can use height already created by a longer title or URL in the same row."]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[150,345,117,107],"idea":"Protect the longest unbreakable URL segment and keep the date and status columns at their one-line widths, accepting substantial title wrapping."},{"name":"B","widths":[210,345,90,74],"idea":"Give titles more room while preserving space for the longest unbreakable URL segment, allowing the audit headers and potentially dates to wrap."},{"name":"C","widths":[180,390,85,64],"idea":"Prioritize the URL for easier destination reading, with a moderate title column and compact audit columns that may require header and date wrapping."}]}
